blocks.content: This chapter is a consolidated, rapid fire review of the questions that come up over and over again in real operating systems interviews, each one pointing back to the dedicated chapter that covers it in full depth. Treat this as a final self check: if any answer here feels shaky, that is exactly the signal to go back and revisit that specific chapter before an actual interview.
Every question below is genuinely common, not hypothetical, these are the exact areas that repeatedly separate a confident, well prepared answer from a shaky, half remembered one.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409395289-611692337.png
1. Process vs Thread

This is very often the very first OS question asked, precisely because a strong answer requires connecting several ideas at once rather than reciting a definition. A process has its own independent address space, its own page table, and is comparatively expensive to create and to switch between, since a context switch between processes generally means changing that page table mapping entirely.

A thread instead shares its address space, its heap, and its open files with every other thread in the same process, covered in full in the threads in Linux chapter, making thread creation and thread to thread switching considerably cheaper, at the real cost of needing explicit synchronization whenever multiple threads touch the same shared data.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409395290-320087426.png
2. The Four Necessary Conditions for Deadlock
blocks.text: 2. The Four Necessary Conditions for Deadlock

blocks.content: Interviewers ask this constantly because it tests whether a candidate actually understands deadlock as a precise, structural phenomenon rather than a vague notion of processes being stuck. All four conditions, mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait, must hold simultaneously for a deadlock to actually occur, covered in complete depth in the four necessary conditions chapter.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409395291-701314985.png
blocks.alt: The Four Necessary Conditions for Deadlock

blocks.content: A strong follow up answer connects this directly to prevention: deadlock prevention strategies each work by deliberately breaking exactly one of these four conditions, and being able to name a concrete prevention technique for each condition shows real mastery, not just memorized terminology.

{"headers":["Condition","A concrete way to break it"],"rows":[["Mutual exclusion","Use resources that can genuinely be shared, where possible, avoiding exclusive locking altogether"],["Hold and wait","Require a process to request all the resources it will need at once, up front"],["No preemption","Allow a resource to be forcibly taken back from a process holding it"],["Circular wait","Impose a strict global ordering on resource acquisition"]]}
3. Paging and Virtual Memory

Be ready to explain, in a clean, confident sentence, that a logical address generated by the CPU gets translated into a physical RAM address by the MMU using the page table, and that this translation is what allows a process address space to be scattered across non contiguous physical frames while still appearing perfectly contiguous to the program itself.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409395291-636267454.png

A frequent, genuinely important follow up is explaining what a page fault actually is, and specifically distinguishing a minor fault from a major fault from an invalid fault, covered in full in the page faults chapter, since this exact three way distinction trips up a large fraction of candidates who only vaguely remember page faults as a single, undifferentiated concept.
4. Mutex vs Semaphore vs Monitor

This comparison is asked constantly, and the cleanest way to answer it is by ownership. A mutex is a binary lock with a strict ownership rule, only the thread that acquired it is allowed to release it. A semaphore is a more general counter that any thread can signal, not necessarily the same one that waited on it, making it suitable for producer consumer style coordination, not just mutual exclusion.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409395292-196049945.png

A monitor bundles a mutex together with condition variables into one higher level, language supported construct, reducing the chance of common mistakes like forgetting to release a lock, covered in full in the monitor chapter.
5. Comparing the CPU Scheduling Algorithms

Be ready to compare FCFS, SJF, priority scheduling, and round robin along consistent axes: average waiting time, fairness, and starvation risk. FCFS is simple but can suffer the convoy effect, a short process stuck waiting behind a long one. SJF minimizes average waiting time optimally but requires predicting burst time in advance, which is not always realistic. Round robin guarantees fairness through time slicing and structurally prevents starvation, at some cost to average turnaround for longer jobs.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785409395292-842483554.png

{"headers":["Algorithm","Strongest property","Real weakness"],"rows":[["FCFS","Simplicity, trivially fair in arrival order","Convoy effect, one long process delays everything behind it"],["SJF","Optimal average waiting time","Requires knowing or predicting burst time in advance"],["Round robin","Fairness, no starvation, good responsiveness","Higher average turnaround for longer jobs than SJF"]]}

blocks.content: ["What happens if a process calls wait but has no children at all. It returns immediately with an error, there is nothing to actually wait for, this is not a hang or a fault.","Can two threads corrupt shared data even if a mutex exists somewhere in the program. Yes, if either thread accesses the shared data without actually acquiring that mutex first, a lock only protects the code that explicitly uses it.","Does closing a file descriptor always free the underlying file resource immediately. No, tying back to the file operations chapter, only once every duplicated or inherited descriptor pointing at the same open file table entry has been closed."]
items: What happens if a process calls wait but has no children at all. It returns immediately with an error, there is nothing to actually wait for, this is not a hang or a fault.

Can two threads corrupt shared data even if a mutex exists somewhere in the program. Yes, if either thread accesses the shared data without actually acquiring that mutex first, a lock only protects the code that explicitly uses it.

Does closing a file descriptor always free the underlying file resource immediately. No, tying back to the file operations chapter, only once every duplicated or inherited descriptor pointing at the same open file table entry has been closed.

blocks.content: The real value of a consolidated review chapter like this one is diagnostic, not a substitute for the dedicated chapters themselves. If an explanation above feels immediately obvious and easy to expand on with a concrete example, that topic is genuinely solid. If it feels like a memorized sentence with no real intuition behind it, that is exactly the signal to revisit the full chapter it points back to before relying on it in an actual interview.

blocks.title: How to use this chapter effectively
blocks.content: Do not simply memorize the short answers given here. For each one, practice explaining it out loud with a concrete example, and if you cannot, that is precisely the topic to revisit in its full dedicated chapter before an interview, not this summary.

blocks.title: The pattern behind good OS answers
blocks.content: The strongest interview answers in this entire subject consistently connect a mechanism to the specific problem it solves, not just its name. Explaining that a mutex exists specifically to prevent a race condition on shared data is a stronger answer than simply defining what a mutex is.

items: Giving a definition without a concrete example, most interviewers are specifically listening for whether a candidate can apply a concept, not just recite it.

Confusing closely related but distinct terms under interview pressure, process versus thread, minor versus major page fault, mutex versus semaphore, these specific pairs come up constantly precisely because they are easy to blur together.
